headline: High-risk shared-write orchestration plus sensitive-data handling creates default-path leakage and cascading errors; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A can read/write application-defined files and uses a checkpointer store; Agent B also reads/writes files and processes notebook/API content. A shared workspace or checkpointed outputs could let B treat A’s generated content as trusted instructions. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred and kept at medium.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or checkpoint store, A’s outputs can be consumed by B as instructions.
IF B ingests A-produced files without provenance checks, prompt injection becomes feasible.
mitigations: Separate workspaces and checkpoint stores per agent.
Add provenance tags to all A outputs before B reads them.
Require B to ignore instruction-like text in files.
Review any shared filesystem mounts before running.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization or schema validation between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A handles model provider API keys and B handles JINA, Telegram, and Langfuse secrets; both have filesystem access and broad/allowlisted egress. If they share a workspace or logs, secrets or paper data can flow between them and out to external services. The pairwise leak path is plausible in default development setups, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF A and B share a filesystem, secrets written by one can be read by the other.
IF either agent logs prompts or files to external APIs, sensitive data can leave the local environment.
mitigations: Store secrets in separate env files per agent.
Disable verbose logging for both agents.
Mount read-only inputs where possible.
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately.
requires-engineering: isolate network egress per agent and per secret class.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shells, spawn subprocesses, read/write filesystems, and use network egress. A’s checkpointer-based shared state and B’s local development/docker-compose workflow create a realistic chance of concurrent writes to the same mutable resources. Because defaults can be dangerous and conflicts may corrupt state, high is appropriate.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory or database, concurrent writes can race.
IF either agent mutates shared config or generated artifacts without locks, state corruption is possible.
mitigations: Assign distinct output directories.
Run only one writer at a time.
Add file locks around shared artifacts.
Snapshot state before each run.
requires-engineering: introduce transactional coordination for shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A is a stateful orchestration framework that can emit intermediate outputs; B is a content-writing agent with API endpoints for ask/stream/agentic-ask. If B consumes A’s outputs as authoritative without verification, errors can cascade into downstream writing or actions. The interaction is plausible from the profiles alone, so high is justified.
conditions: IF B uses A-generated text or state as source material, mistakes can propagate.
IF B performs downstream publishing or API-driven actions from A’s outputs, the blast radius expands.
mitigations: Insert a human review step before B acts on A outputs.
Require citations or source links for A-derived claims.
Compare A outputs against original sources.
Limit B to drafting only.
requires-engineering: add automated verification gates before downstream actions.

E_compliance.rationale: A touches graph state and model-provider keys; B touches academic papers, paper metadata, research questions, and configuration secrets. The profiles do not show a direct residency mismatch, but they do show different retention-sensitive data classes and secret handling. That creates a compliance gap if the pair shares logs or storage, so medium fits.
conditions: IF shared logs retain paper metadata or secrets longer than intended, retention policy mismatch occurs.
IF EU or regulated data is routed through external services without a DPA, compliance risk increases.
mitigations: Document retention for both agents.
Separate regulated data from general logs.
Purge temporary files after each run.
Confirm vendor DPAs for external services.
requires-engineering: implement policy-based data routing and retention controls.
